node-1.label: An 80-year-old woman presented with difficulty raising her right upper limb, progressive dyskinesia, gait disorder, neck pain, and numbness in her extremities

node-2.label: She had neck pain for approximately 2 years and numbness in her extremities for about 1 year, both significantly worsened before her visit; she could walk unassisted for less than 100 meters

node-3.label: Physical examination showed muscle weakness (MMT score 3) in the entire right upper limb, normal strength in the remaining limbs, hypesthesia throughout the upper and lower limbs, increased deep tendon reflexes bilaterally in all limbs, positive Hoffman's and Wartenberg's signs, and preoperative JOA score 8.5 points

node-4.label: Radiographs and cervical contrast CT revealed osteolytic lesions in C3-7; a mass extended into the spinal canal from within the vertebrae, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side; the mass was stained in the early contrast phase and showed an internal low-density area; MRI detected a mass with the same signal profile as bone from within the C3-7 vertebrae to outside of the vertebral bodies, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side at the same levels

node-5.label: Blood tests showed no thrombocytopenia, anemia, or coagulation abnormalities; inflammatory response was normal; blood cultures and various tumor markers were negative; percutaneous vertebral biopsy showed culture negativity and no neoplastic lesions

attrs.why: New pathologist and radiologist analyses report that the retrieved biopsy shows atypical vasoforming proliferation with ERG/CD31/CD34 positivity, pericytic myo1B/CD146/SMA positivity, negative D2-40/CAMTA1/TFE3/FOSB, Ki-67 16.1%/10.6%, and infiltration into surrounding muscle and fat, favoring vascular neoplasm. Imaging shows osteolytic C3-7 lesions with cord compression and contrast staining. These findings substantially increase the likelihood of cervical spine neoplasm and outweigh the earlier negative biopsy interpretation; confidence is raised from 0.4 to 0.8.

Negative blood cultures, normal inflammatory markers, and culture-negative biopsy already argued against infection/inflammation. The new expert analyses and biopsy immunophenotype showing atypical vasoforming proliferation with vascular markers now favor a vascular neoplasm rather than an infectious/inflammatory process. Confidence is decreased from 0.15 to 0.08.

The new expert analyses and biopsy findings of atypical vasoforming proliferation, ERG/CD31/CD34 and pericytic marker positivity, high Ki-67, and infiltration into surrounding muscle/fat favor a vascular neoplasm and explicitly suggest the non-neoplastic bone lesion probability should be downregulated. Although osteolytic C3-7 changes and cord compression remain, these biopsy features refute a non-neoplastic bone lesion; confidence is reduced from 0.45 to 0.12.

The frontier 'cervical spine vascular neoplasm' is a broad category rather than a specific entity. Biopsy (node-9/10) shows atypical vasoforming proliferation with endothelial ERG/CD31/CD34 positivity, and node-11/12 document Ki-67 of 10.6–16.1% and infiltration into muscle/fat (node-12), which are features of a malignant vascular tumor; negativity for FOSB/CAMTA1/TFE3 (node-10) does not exclude angiosarcoma, making it a plausible fine-grained subtype.

An intermediate-malignancy vasoforming tumor consistent with the frontier and with the locally aggressive behavior in node-16; however, the negative CAMTA1 and TFE3 (node-10) argues against classic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, so it remains a less favored but possible refinement.

Vertebral hemangioma is the most common vascular lesion of the spine, and node-4 shows an osteolytic C3-7 mass with early-phase contrast staining; yet the biopsy atypia (node-9) and elevated Ki-67 (node-11) argue against a simple benign hemangioma, so this is a low-probability refinement of the frontier.
A vascular neoplasm that can arise in the spine and would fit the frontier, but node-10 shows D2-40 negativity and there is no VHL context, making hemangioblastoma a less likely fine-grained subtype.

A vascular tumor sharing endothelial marker positivity with the frontier, but HHV8 status is unknown and the clinical setting is atypical, so this is a rare possible subtype of the vascular neoplasm hypothesis.
